# **Stargazer: User Needs and Market Landscape for Public Lunar Exploration Tools**

**Generated by MiroThinker2026-11-14**

---

**11\. Executive Summary**

Educators, students and the general public are strongly interested in the Moon and upcoming lunar missions, but they struggle with *spatially complex*, *time‑varying* lunar concepts such as phases, illumination cycles, terrain and Earth visibility. Multiple studies show high rates of misconceptions about lunar phases and illumination among both students and teachers[**\[1\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187118431630049X)**[\[2\]](https://www.nsta.org/science-teacher/science-teacher-january-2013/moon-misconceptions)[\[3\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198983)[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/moon_lunar_phases/)[\[5\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa9b0d)**, while research on map reading and topography finds persistent difficulty in interpreting 2D representations of 3D terrain[**\[6\]**](https://serc.carleton.edu/NAGTWorkshops/visualization/teaching_geospatial/topo_maps.html). Existing NASA tools like Moon Trek and QuickMap are powerful and widely used in education and outreach[**\[7\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/jpl/config/textAbout.html)**[\[8\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/)[\[9\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20170001701)[\[10\]](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/quickmap)[\[11\]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016AGUFMED43E..04T/abstract)**, yet official descriptions and challenge briefs explicitly note that they are “built for detailed analysis” and often too complex for non‑specialists to use for rapid comparisons[**\[12\]**](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/)**[\[13\]](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/details/)**.

For Stargazer, the opportunity is not to out‑compete NASA on data depth, but to become the *translation layer* between mission‑grade tools and public understanding: a focused, scenario‑driven interface that makes a small number of key questions—“Why this site?”, “When is it lit?”, “Can you see Earth from here?”—visually obvious and narratively explained.

Key cross‑cutting implications:

* **Core user need:** connect high‑fidelity lunar data to *intuitive, story‑driven visual explanations* that correct misconceptions about illumination, phases, and visibility.  
* **Design priority:** simple, guided 3D experiences with linked perspectives (from orbit and from the surface) and time sliders, rather than exposing full expert toolsets.  
* **Differentiation space:** rapid, side‑by‑side landing‑site comparison with time‑based sunlight/Earth‑visibility, plus embedded, teacher‑ready explanations and activities. This is explicitly requested in the Space Apps “Lunar Landing Site Navigator” brief[**\[13\]**](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/details/)\[14\].  
* **Adoption levers:** standards‑aligned classroom activities, turnkey museum/exhibit modes, and alignment with widely promoted events like Artemis missions and International Observe the Moon Night[**\[15\]**](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017AGUFMED53H0231B/abstract)**[\[16\]](https://moon.nasa.gov/observe-the-moon-night/)**.

The most actionable takeaway: **build Stargazer as a story‑centric, teacher‑friendly “mission planning sandbox” for non‑experts**, not a general‑purpose GIS. Every feature should shorten the path from “I’m curious about this site” to “I can explain, in plain language, why its lighting and visibility matter.”

---

**22\. Target Audience Needs**

### **2.1 Educators**

**Conceptual pain points.** Astronomy education research consistently shows that teachers themselves hold misconceptions about lunar phases, illumination and the Earth‑Moon‑Sun system[**\[1\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187118431630049X)**[\[2\]](https://www.nsta.org/science-teacher/science-teacher-january-2013/moon-misconceptions)[\[3\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198983)[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/moon_lunar_phases/)[\[5\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa9b0d)**. Studies of pre‑service and in‑service teachers report large fractions attributing phases to Earth’s shadow, conflating phases with eclipses, or mis‑stating the length and nature of the lunar day[**\[1\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187118431630049X)**[\[3\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198983)[\[5\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa9b0d)[\[17\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/)**. Teachers also report low confidence in their own spatial‑scientific reasoning and note that this affects what and how they teach about lunar topics[**\[18\]**](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa9d16). This means educators need *tools that teach them while they teach*—visualizations tightly coupled with robust explanatory scaffolding.

**Spatial and representational challenges.** Teacher guides from agencies like the Canadian Space Agency and NASA emphasize that the movements and relative scales in the Earth‑Moon‑Sun system are hard to represent and to mentally visualize[**\[6\]**](https://serc.carleton.edu/NAGTWorkshops/visualization/teaching_geospatial/topo_maps.html)**[\[19\]](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/educators/resources/moon/)**. The LRO Educator Resource Kit explicitly notes that it is “difficult to look at a lunar image and decide” features such as slope and landform type[**\[20\]**](https://lunar.gsfc.nasa.gov/educators/lro_educator_kit.pdf), underscoring that 2D imagery alone is not didactically sufficient. Teachers gravitate toward physical or interactive models when available[**\[3\]**](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198983)**[\[21\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1185471)**, suggesting high receptivity to a digital 3D tool that behaves like a manipulable model.

**Motivations and curriculum drivers.** Educators are actively seeking ways to connect Artemis and renewed lunar exploration to standards‑aligned classroom content. NASA, LPI and others provide K‑12 lunar curricula, hands‑on challenges and Artemis‑linked activities[**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[23\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/moon/)[\[24\]](https://www.nasa.gov/stem/multimedia/moon-to-mars.html)**. A K12 Dive article and NASA resources describe using upcoming missions to teach media literacy, cross‑curricular connections (geology, engineering, history) and critical thinking[**\[25\]**](https://www.k12dive.com/news/3-ways-upcoming-lunar-missions-can-engage-students/703035/)**[\[26\]](https://www.nasa.gov/stem/artemisforstudents)**. Adoption is thus driven by:

* Alignment with existing curriculum strands (Earth–space systems, light and shadows, maps and scale, engineering design).  
* Turnkey lesson structures: pre‑built activities, prompts and assessments rather than just raw tools.  
* Evidence that tools improve conceptual understanding or engagement; NASA’s Infiniscope, for example, is explicitly framed around evaluated interactive experiences for Moon phases[**\[27\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/resources/nasa-science-for-your-classroom-opportunities-for-educators/).

**What would make an interactive lunar tool useful for educators.**

From existing resources and tool usage patterns:

* **Linked perspectives and manipulable models.** PBS LearningMedia’s lunar phases simulation—viewing the system simultaneously from Earth and from space—explicitly targets cause‑and‑effect understanding and spatial/time scales[**\[28\]**](https://www.pbslearningmedia.org/resource/buac19-35-sci-ess-earthsunmoon35model/moon-phases-simulation-viewed-from-earth-and-space/)**[\[29\]](https://www.pbs.org/education/blogs/pbs-in-the-classroom/launch-your-class-to-the-moon-and-back/)**. Teachers value this dual‑perspective capability as it mirrors recommended pedagogy.  
* **Guided inquiry structures.** Many NASA and LPI resources embed simulations within structured guided‑inquiry or project‑based units[**\[3\]**](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198983)**[\[22\]](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)[\[27\]](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/resources/nasa-science-for-your-classroom-opportunities-for-educators/)**, rather than expecting teachers to design activities from scratch.  
* **Accessibility and device constraints.** School infrastructure often relies on mixed or older devices. Tools like QuickMap require substantial processing power and modern graphics[**\[30\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/quickmap/help), which can limit classroom use; educators need web‑based tools that run smoothly on mid‑range laptops and Chromebooks.  
* **Assessment support.** Astronomy education tools increasingly include embedded quizzes or formative checks[**\[31\]**](https://www.nsta.org/science-scope/science-scope-january-2019/moon-phases)**[\[32\]](https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/moons/earths-moon/in-depth/)**. Even basic self‑check questions around a visualization help teachers gauge learning without separate systems.

### **2.2 Students**

**What students want to know.** Surveys and education content reveal that students are naturally curious about:

* What the Moon’s surface is like: terrain, craters, “dark side,” and whether it’s dusty, rocky, etc.[**\[33\]**](https://www.csiro.au/en/research/space/space-science/moon-facts).  
* Temperature, day–night cycles, and what it would be like to stand at a particular location (sunrise/sunset length, darkness)[**\[33\]**](https://www.csiro.au/en/research/space/space-science/moon-facts)**[\[17\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/)[\[32\]](https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/moons/earths-moon/in-depth/)**.  
* Why humans choose certain landing sites; what makes a “good” site in terms of safety, resources, and communications[**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[24\]](https://www.nasa.gov/stem/multimedia/moon-to-mars.html)[\[34\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/moonScience/UnknownMoon.pdf)**.  
* How Artemis and future missions differ from Apollo, and what future lunar bases might look like[**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[25\]](https://www.k12dive.com/news/3-ways-upcoming-lunar-missions-can-engage-students/703035/)**.

**Conceptual difficulties and misconceptions.** Multiple studies across grades report:

* Confusion about lunar illumination: phases attributed to Earth’s shadow, belief that the Moon makes its own light, or that phases depend on observer location on Earth[**\[1\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187118431630049X)**[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/moon_lunar_phases/)[\[5\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa9b0d)[\[31\]](https://www.nsta.org/science-scope/science-scope-january-2019/moon-phases)[\[35\]](https://www.nsta.org/blog/common-moon-misconceptions)**.  
* Failure to grasp that the Moon is always half‑lit by the Sun; the phases arise from changing viewing angles, not changing illumination[**\[29\]**](https://www.pbs.org/education/blogs/pbs-in-the-classroom/launch-your-class-to-the-moon-and-back/)**[\[36\]](https://www.pbslearningmedia.org/resource/lsps07-sci-ess-halfmoon/always-half-full/)**.  
* Conflation of lunar phases with day–night cycles; many students do not appreciate that the lunar synodic day is about a month with long continuous day and night periods[**\[17\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/)**[\[32\]](https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/moons/earths-moon/in-depth/)**.  
* Difficulty with scale and spatial relationships (Earth–Moon distance, sizes, orbits) and with interpreting 3D arrangements from 2D diagrams[**\[6\]**](https://serc.carleton.edu/NAGTWorkshops/visualization/teaching_geospatial/topo_maps.html)**[\[8\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/)[\[37\]](https://doi.org/10.1002/tea.20322)**.

These issues are tightly connected to weaknesses in spatial thinking skills; research finds moderate correlations between spatial ability and understanding of lunar phases[**\[8\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/)**[\[38\]](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/12/5/359)**.

**What motivates students.** Beyond innate curiosity, documented motivators include:

* **Narrative and role‑play.** Activities where students assume roles (e.g., engineer in “Lunar Nautics” or mission‑planning games) increase engagement and link abstract science to personal agency[**\[39\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/lunar_nautics/)**[\[40\]](https://www.mosi.org/things-to-do/mission-moonbase/)**.  
* **Connections to real missions and current events.** Artemis launches, lunar heritage (Apollo sites), and live events like International Observe the Moon Night are used as hooks to foster interest and media literacy[**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[25\]](https://www.k12dive.com/news/3-ways-upcoming-lunar-missions-can-engage-students/703035/)[\[41\]](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/30/science/nasa-astronauts-moon-americans-mood.html)**.  
* **Immersive and interactive technology.** Studies indicate that students using 3D visualization tools (e.g., WorldWide Telescope) show higher learning gains and enthusiasm than those using 2D simulators[**\[38\]**](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/12/5/359)**[\[42\]](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/international-journal-of-astronomy-education/article/worldwide-telescope-in-education/)**. Interactive model manipulation supports self‑discovery of mechanisms behind moon phases and eclipses[**\[2\]**](https://www.nsta.org/science-teacher/science-teacher-january-2013/moon-misconceptions)**[\[29\]](https://www.pbs.org/education/blogs/pbs-in-the-classroom/launch-your-class-to-the-moon-and-back/)**.

**What would make Stargazer valuable to students.**

Students benefit most when they can:

* *Manipulate* time and viewpoint to see direct cause–effect relationships (e.g., how orbit and rotation convert into changing illumination and Earth visibility).  
* Immediately relate visuals to “what would it be like if I were there?” (shadow lengths, horizon appearance, seeing Earth low or high in the sky).  
* Share or present their own findings (screenshots, annotated views) for projects or presentations.

### **2.3 General Public**

**Interest levels and themes.** Public opinion data from 2026 surveys show strong ongoing interest in space exploration. One national poll in June 2026 reported roughly two‑thirds of Americans interested in space and large majorities expecting humans to return to the Moon and even mine space resources in the coming decades[**\[43\]**](https://www.leonarddavid.com/public-interest-in-space-revealing-new-survey/). At the same time, longitudinal data indicate space exploration is a lower policy priority than domestic issues[**\[44\]**](https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2023/03/28/public-views-of-nasas-future/), suggesting that *passive interest is high, but attention is scarce*.

Exhibit design and outreach practices show what captures public attention:

* **Immersive visuals and physical scale.** Traveling Moon sculpture exhibits using high‑resolution NASA imagery—like Luke Jerram’s “Museum of the Moon”—draw strong public engagement by allowing people to “stand under” or walk around a large‑scale Moon[**\[45\]**](https://my-moon.org/)**[\[46\]](https://www.exploratorium.edu/visit/calendar/museum-of-the-moon)**.  
* **Interactive, open‑ended experiences.** Science museums increasingly use digital media and interactive stations to support deeper learning, emphasizing technological novelty and open‑ended exploration[**\[47\]**](https://www.thinglink.com/blog/how-museums-are-using-interactive-media-to-boost-visitor-engagement/)**[\[48\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1231234.1231245)**. Lunar exhibits like “Mission Moonbase” let visitors role‑play scientists/engineers and interact with models[**\[40\]**](https://www.mosi.org/things-to-do/mission-moonbase/).  
* **Simple, compelling questions.** Public‑facing resources emphasize accessible questions: Where did Apollo land? Where will Artemis land? Why those places? What does it look like from there? Can you see Earth? What happens to sunlight in crater shadows?[**\[33\]**](https://www.csiro.au/en/research/space/space-science/moon-facts)**[\[49\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/interactives/)[\[50\]](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/featured_sites)**.

**Barriers and needs.**

For non‑specialists:

* **Cognitive overload.** Tools that expose many data layers, projections and analysis options (e.g., QuickMap, Moon Trek, Google Moon) can overwhelm curiosity‑driven users; even professional articles acknowledge that many astronomy tools are “unnecessarily difficult to use,” which “inhibits casual inquiry”[**\[12\]**](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/).  
* **Jargon and context gaps.** Terms like “libration,” “sub‑Earth point,” “LOLA DEM” or “illumination fraction” are not self‑explanatory; without interpretation, they remain opaque data overlays.  
* **Device and access constraints.** General users often access content on mobile devices; some current tools are desktop‑centric, involve plugins, or offer sub‑optimal mobile usability[**\[51\]**](https://www.cnet.com/reviews/worldwide-telescope-review/)**[\[52\]](https://www.facebook.com/WorldWideTelescope/posts/)**.

Public users therefore need a *frictionless entry point*—a browser‑based experience with:

* Immediate visual payoff (e.g., a famous landing site with a short narrative).  
* Minimal required controls, with optional “more detail” for those who want to dive deeper.  
* Clear narrative framing of “why this matters” for mission safety, communication, or science.

---

**33\. Problems and Frustrations**

This section consolidates cross‑audience difficulties relevant to Stargazer’s scope.

### **3.1 Misconceptions and Conceptual Barriers**

* **Lunar phases and illumination.** Studies of students and preservice teachers document that large fractions attribute phases to Earth’s shadow, believe the Moon makes its own light, or think the phases vary by observer location[**\[1\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187118431630049X)**[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/moon_lunar_phases/)[\[5\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa9b0d)[\[31\]](https://www.nsta.org/science-scope/science-scope-january-2019/moon-phases)[\[35\]](https://www.nsta.org/blog/common-moon-misconceptions)**. These misconceptions persist even after conventional instruction[**\[2\]**](https://www.nsta.org/science-teacher/science-teacher-january-2013/moon-misconceptions)**[\[31\]](https://www.nsta.org/science-scope/science-scope-january-2019/moon-phases)**.  
* **Lunar day/night cycles.** Research on prospective teachers and educational resources highlight confusion about the length and structure of the lunar day, with many failing to grasp that a typical location experiences \~14 Earth days of sunlight followed by \~14 days of darkness[**\[17\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/)**[\[32\]](https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/moons/earths-moon/in-depth/)**.  
* **Earth‑Moon‑Sun system and scale.** Multiple sources underline that learners struggle to visualize 3D motion, relative scale, and perspective in the system[**\[6\]**](https://serc.carleton.edu/NAGTWorkshops/visualization/teaching_geospatial/topo_maps.html)**[\[8\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/)[\[19\]](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/educators/resources/moon/)[\[37\]](https://doi.org/10.1002/tea.20322)**. Without this, illumination patterns, visibility constraints and libration are unintuitive.

### **3.2 Spatial Visualization and Topography**

* **Interpreting 2D maps and terrains.** Geoscience education research shows students frequently misinterpret contour maps and other 2D topographic representations, struggling with elevation, slope, and shape[**\[6\]**](https://serc.carleton.edu/NAGTWorkshops/visualization/teaching_geospatial/topo_maps.html). Lunar resources similarly note the difficulty of understanding south polar topography from flat maps or globes[**\[53\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/specials/artemis-south-pole-atlas/).  
* **Terrain‑dependent visibility.** Studies of Earth visibility from lunar polar regions show that terrain can obscure Earth for large fractions of time, and that spherical models over‑estimate visibility[**\[54\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0094576519308925). This is an inherently 3D, line‑of‑sight phenomenon that text descriptions or static maps convey poorly.

### **3.3 Usability and Accessibility of Existing Tools**

* **Expert‑oriented complexity.** The Space Apps “Lunar Landing Site Navigator” challenge explicitly states that current tools which provide the necessary information—NASA’s QuickMap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons—are “built for detailed analysis” and “often difficult for non‑specialists” to use effectively, especially for rapid comparison tasks[**\[12\]**](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/)**[\[13\]](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/details/)**. A related paper echoes that lunar mapping tools are “difficult to access, even for experts”[**\[55\]**](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/21681376.2019.1577300).  
* **Steep learning curves and performance demands.** QuickMap is described by NASA as a powerful 2D/3D interface for browsing LRO data[**\[10\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/quickmap), but documentation and community notes mention significant processing demands and note that it was tailored for scientists and other professional stakeholders[**\[56\]**](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013LPSC...44.2415W/abstract). Some discussion threads and technical memos about older or related tools (e.g., LTVT) mention platform limitations (Windows‑only), fixed viewing windows, and limitations in realistic shadow simulation[**\[57\]**](https://www.cloudynights.com/topic/597915-lroc-quickmap-lighting/)**[\[58\]](http://ltvt.wikispaces.com/)**.  
* **Fragmentation of functionality.** Earth visibility maps, sun visibility maps, engineering illumination tools (e.g., DLES/DVT), Apollo site browsers and south pole atlases are scattered across different platforms[**\[9\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20170001701)**[\[53\]](https://www.nasa.gov/specials/artemis-south-pole-atlas/)[\[54\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0094576519308925)[\[59\]](https://lunar.gsfc.nasa.gov/educators/earth_visibility.pdf)**. Educators or public users wanting to answer integrated questions (“Where is well‑lit, with Earth in view, and why was that chosen?”) must traverse multiple tools.

### **3.4 Gaps in Explanation and Pedagogical Support**

* **Data without narrative.** Moon Trek and QuickMap provide hundreds of data products, from DEMs to compositional maps, plus measurement tools[**\[7\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/jpl/config/textAbout.html)**[\[9\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20170001701)[\[10\]](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/quickmap)**. For educators and the public, the data richness is undercut by limited in‑context explanation of why given datasets matter to landing‑site decisions or to everyday questions (“Will there be power and communication here?”).  
* **Lack of structured guidance for novices.** Although training materials, tutorials and lesson plans exist around these tools, much of the on‑screen experience assumes a user already knows what to look for. In contrast, dedicated educational platforms like Infiniscope wrap visualizations in structured narratives and tasks[**\[27\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/resources/nasa-science-for-your-classroom-opportunities-for-educators/).

Collectively, these problems point toward the same design thesis: **the binding constraint is not access to data, but conversion of expert analyses into cognitively manageable, guided visual stories.**

---

**44\. Existing Tools and Competitor Analysis**

This section focuses on tools and resources most relevant to Stargazer’s feature set.

### **4.1 NASA Moon Trek (Solar System Treks)**

**Purpose and capabilities.** Moon Trek is NASA’s web‑based portal for lunar exploration, part of the Solar System Treks suite. It provides interactive visualization and analysis tools, including:

* High‑resolution imagery and DEMs from LRO and other missions.  
* 2D and 3D views, fly‑over and navigation, measurement tools, data layering, and 3D model export[**\[7\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/jpl/config/textAbout.html)**[\[9\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20170001701)[\[11\]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016AGUFMED43E..04T/abstract)[\[60\]](https://moon.nasa.gov/observe-the-moon-night/resources/moon-trek/)**.  
* Support for mission planning, scientific research, commercial users, and education/outreach[**\[7\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/jpl/config/textAbout.html)**[\[8\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/)[\[11\]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016AGUFMED43E..04T/abstract)[\[61\]](https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/leag2016/pdf/5015.pdf)**.

Moon Trek is publicly accessible in the browser without registration and is used in contexts ranging from high‑school research programs (e.g., ExMASS) to public engagement in Moon‑focused events[**\[7\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/jpl/config/textAbout.html)**[\[8\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/)[\[15\]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017AGUFMED53H0231B/abstract)[\[62\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/exploration/education/hsResearch/lunar_data/)**.

**Strengths.**

* **Data authority and breadth.** Backed by JPL and LRO data; integrates hundreds of data products with metadata[**\[7\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/jpl/config/textAbout.html)**[\[9\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20170001701)**.  
* **Flexibility.** Serves mission planners and scientists while also being recommended in educational kits and PBS resources[**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[52\]](https://www.facebook.com/WorldWideTelescope/posts/)**.  
* **Continuous enhancement.** Recent interfaces emphasize improved navigation, performance and reliability[**\[11\]**](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016AGUFMED43E..04T/abstract), and NASA actively runs UX studies to improve it[**\[63\]**](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/events/moon-trek-user-experience-study).

**Limitations for Stargazer’s audiences.**

* **Expert‑first design.** Core positioning remains mission planning and analysis; many controls (projections, data products, tools) are irrelevant or confusing for novice users.  
* **Steep initial learning curve.** NASA and partner descriptions highlight Moon Trek as powerful and feature‑rich, but independent materials and the Space Apps brief still classify it among tools “built for detailed analysis” and challenging for non‑specialists to use for rapid, comparative tasks[**\[12\]**](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/)**[\[13\]](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/details/)**.  
* **Limited narrative framing on‑screen.** Tutorial materials and external lesson plans exist, but the UI itself does not foreground stories like “Why this south pole ridge is favorable” in plain language.

**Implications for Stargazer.** Rather than replicating Moon Trek, Stargazer can:

* Consume the same or similar data, but present only a *small curated subset* relevant to landing‑site comparison.  
* Provide opinionated workflows that answer a few high‑value questions, sacrificing generality for clarity.  
* Position itself as a “front porch” that could link out to Moon Trek for deeper data exploration.

### **4.2 LROC QuickMap and Related Lunar Data Tools**

**Purpose and capabilities.** LROC QuickMap is a web‑based viewer for browsing LRO and other lunar datasets in 2D and 3D[**\[10\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/quickmap). It supports scientists, educators and commercial stakeholders with tools for measurements, data layering, and export[**\[10\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/quickmap)**[\[56\]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013LPSC...44.2415W/abstract)**. The LRO Educator Resource Kit and associated activities use QuickMap and related tools for student research projects[**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[55\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/21681376.2019.1577300)**.

**Strengths.**

* **High‑fidelity data and scientific credibility.**  
* **Rich tooling for professional and student research**: measurements, profiles, lighting controls.  
* **Integration into educational projects** (e.g., high‑school lunar geology research)[**\[55\]**](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/21681376.2019.1577300).

**Limitations for non‑experts.**

* **Performance and complexity barriers.** QuickMap’s 3D engine and data volume demand modern hardware and recent graphics drivers; some documentation indicates older or small devices may struggle[**\[30\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/quickmap/help). Controls and layering options can feel overwhelming for beginners.  
* **Shadow/illumination simulation limitations for South Pole work.** Community discussions and documentation note QuickMap’s lighting controls weren’t designed as a full physical shadow simulator and have issues at extreme zenith angles[**\[57\]**](https://www.cloudynights.com/topic/597915-lroc-quickmap-lighting/), which undermines intuitive exploration of extreme polar lighting scenarios.

**Implications for Stargazer.** QuickMap is a back‑end benchmark: if Stargazer relies on LRO datasets, it must be *lighter* and *simpler* than QuickMap and should avoid duplicating advanced measurement features. It can instead deliver:

* Pre‑computed, narrative‑ready illumination and visibility views.  
* Simple controls that wrap complex illumination computations behind a time slider and explanatory text.

### **4.3 Other Visualization and Educational Platforms**

#### 4.3.1 South Pole Atlases, Earth/Sun Visibility Maps and Engineering Tools

NASA and partners provide:

* **Lunar South Pole atlases** with maps, images and illustrations detailing south polar craters and candidate sites[**\[53\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/specials/artemis-south-pole-atlas/).  
* **Educational Earth and Sun visibility maps** in the LRO Educator Resource Kit, where students analyze maps to select suitable base locations[**\[53\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/specials/artemis-south-pole-atlas/)**[\[59\]](https://lunar.gsfc.nasa.gov/educators/earth_visibility.pdf)**.  
* **Engineering visualization tools** such as DLES/DVT that allow exploration of candidate landing/exploration sites over ranges of dates and associated illumination conditions[**\[64\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20205010352)**[\[65\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20190031813)**.  
* **NASA SVS visualizations** showing Earth and Sun visibility from south polar vantage points with realistic motions[**\[54\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0094576519308925)**[\[66\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4655)**.

These tools validate the importance of Stargazer’s planned focus (illumination and Earth visibility over time), but they are either highly technical (DLES/DVT) or packaged as static resources rather than interactive public‑facing apps.

#### 4.3.2 WorldWide Telescope, Stellarium, Virtual Moon Atlas and Planetarium‑Style Tools

WorldWide Telescope (WWT), Stellarium, Celestia and Virtual Moon Atlas occupy the astronomy education / amateur domain:

* WWT offers powerful 3D visualization of planetary systems and has been used in classrooms and public outreach; students using WWT achieved higher learning gains than those using 2D simulators in astronomy education research[**\[38\]**](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/12/5/359)**[\[42\]](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/international-journal-of-astronomy-education/article/worldwide-telescope-in-education/)**.  
* Stellarium is widely used as a cognitive visualization tool to visualize night sky phenomena, improving conceptual understanding when integrated into instruction[**\[67\]**](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10494820.2018.1541913)**[\[68\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1286/1/012022)**; user discussions also highlight UI orientation quirks and complexity for novices[**\[69\]**](https://sourceforge.net/p/stellarium/discussion/278769/thread/).  
* Virtual Moon Atlas is recommended by ESA and education ministries as a detailed lunar atlas, but some descriptions note a steep learning curve for beginners[**\[70\]**](http://ap-i.net/avl/en/start).

These tools demonstrate demand for 3D, exploratory visualization, but their focus is broad celestial navigation or detailed lunar observation; they do not specialize in landing‑site decision narratives or time‑varying illumination/visibility in a mission context.

#### 4.3.3 Museum and Informal Education Interactives

Museums and informal learning environments employ:

* **Interactive lunar exhibits** with multimedia content and augmented reality (“Let’s Quest the Lunar Surface”) designed for children’s learning about the Moon[**\[71\]**](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/276016704).  
* **Immersive mission‑themed installations**, such as “Mission Moonbase” and Moon Shot Museum, where visitors act as scientists/engineers and interact with simulated mission environments[**\[40\]**](https://www.mosi.org/things-to-do/mission-moonbase/)**[\[72\]](https://moonshotmuseum.org/exhibits/)**.  
* **Touchscreen interfaces powered by Moon Trek** in exhibits that allow visitors to explore the lunar surface[**\[73\]**](https://sites.google.com/francis.edu/earth-to-moon/exhibit-components).  
* **NASA “Moon Interactives”** that let users climb virtual lunar mountains, examine samples, and “dig” beneath the surface[**\[49\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/interactives/).

These experiences prioritize:

* Simple, visually striking interactions.  
* Role‑play and narrative framing.  
* Limited but meaningful control surfaces (e.g., a small set of buttons or sliders) tailored to an exhibit storyline.

**Implications for Stargazer.** Stargazer can position itself as a *digital exhibit in a browser*—combining the narrative clarity of museum experiences with the data authenticity of Moon Trek.

---

**55\. Recommended Stargazer Features**

Below, features are grouped roughly by priority. Each section notes primary audiences, target problems, rationale and whether it should be core or optional.

### **5.1 Core Feature: Guided 3D Landing‑Site Explorer with Linked Perspectives**

**Audience.** Educators (especially middle/high‑school), students, curious public.

**User problems addressed.**

* Difficulty visualizing 3D terrain and its relation to illumination and Earth visibility[**\[6\]**](https://serc.carleton.edu/NAGTWorkshops/visualization/teaching_geospatial/topo_maps.html)**[\[53\]](https://www.nasa.gov/specials/artemis-south-pole-atlas/)[\[54\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0094576519308925)**.  
* Misconceptions about phases and illumination driven by weak spatial models of the Earth‑Moon‑Sun system[**\[1\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187118431630049X)**[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/moon_lunar_phases/)[\[8\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/)[\[29\]](https://www.pbs.org/education/blogs/pbs-in-the-classroom/launch-your-class-to-the-moon-and-back/)**.

**Description and rationale.**

* A 3D globe of the Moon with the ability to:  
  * Select a small, curated set of “stories” (e.g., Apollo 11, Artemis south pole site, a permanently shadowed crater, a near‑equatorial site).  
  * View each site from **two synchronized perspectives**:  
    * Orbital or “god’s eye” view showing Sun and Earth directions.  
    * Surface‑level view approximating an astronaut’s horizon.  
* Linked rotation and time sliders allow users to see how shadows and Earth’s apparent position change with time.

Research on lunar phases teaching shows that simultaneous Earth and space perspectives significantly help students recognize cause‑and‑effect relationships and spatial/time scales[**\[28\]**](https://www.pbslearningmedia.org/resource/buac19-35-sci-ess-earthsunmoon35model/moon-phases-simulation-viewed-from-earth-and-space/)**[\[29\]](https://www.pbs.org/education/blogs/pbs-in-the-classroom/launch-your-class-to-the-moon-and-back/)**, while interactive 3D visualization yields better learning gains than 2D views[**\[38\]**](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/12/5/359)**[\[42\]](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/international-journal-of-astronomy-education/article/worldwide-telescope-in-education/)**. Implementing linked perspectives directly operationalizes these insights.

**Priority.** Core. This is the central visualization engine on which most other features can build.

### **5.2 Core Feature: Time Slider for Illumination and Earth Visibility**

**Audience.** All three groups; especially teachers and students.

**User problems addressed.**

* Confusion about lunar day/night structure and long illumination cycles[**\[17\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/)**[\[32\]](https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/moons/earths-moon/in-depth/)**.  
* Difficulty relating static maps to dynamic conditions (e.g., when solar power is available, when Earth is in view)[**\[53\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/specials/artemis-south-pole-atlas/)**[\[54\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0094576519308925)[\[64\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20205010352)**.

**Description and rationale.**

* A time slider (e.g., over several lunar days or a full lunar month) that:  
  * Visually encodes whether the Sun is above the horizon at the site and approximate solar elevation.  
  * Shows if Earth is above the local horizon and its approximate altitude/azimuth.  
* Color‑coded bands or simple icons (Sun up/down; Earth up/down) appear both on the globe and on a small “conditions timeline.”

Engineering tools like DLES/DVT already compute illumination ranges over time for candidate sites[**\[64\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20205010352)**[\[65\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20190031813)**; the Space Apps brief explicitly encourages “animations or timeline views” that show how Sun and Earth positions change over a lunar day\[14\]. Stargazer translates these specialized analyses into an intuitive interface for non‑experts.

**Priority.** Core. This directly addresses one of the most distinctive and educationally rich aspects of lunar exploration.

### **5.3 Core Feature: Landing‑Site Comparison Panel**

**Audience.** Educators, students, public; also fits mission‑planner outreach.

**User problems addressed.**

* Need to compare candidate sites and dates quickly, rather than analyzing each in isolation[**\[13\]**](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/details/)\[14\].  
* Cognitive overload from multi‑tool workflows when trying to compare terrain, illumination and Earth visibility.

**Description and rationale.**

* A comparison mode where users can select 2–3 predefined or user‑chosen sites and see, side by side:  
  * Basic descriptors in plain language (latitude, region name, nearby notable features).  
  * Simple metrics for a given period: proportion of time with Sun above horizon, average solar elevation, proportion of time Earth is visible.  
  * Thumbnail visualizations of terrain (e.g., hillshade or 3D view snapshot).  
* A toggle between “Simple” and “Detailed” comparison to keep general audiences from being overwhelmed.

NASA LROC’s “Featured Sites” already demonstrates public appetite for landing‑site browsing and includes swipe comparisons of imagery across lighting conditions[**\[50\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/featured_sites). The Space Apps challenge calls specifically for intuitive landing‑site and date comparison for mission planners and the public[**\[13\]**](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/details/)\[14\]. Stargazer can differentiate itself via *integrated* comparative views that combine terrain, illumination and visibility.

**Priority.** Core. Comparative capability is central to the stated challenge and value proposition.

### **5.4 Core Feature: Embedded Explanations and Misconception‑Aware Narratives**

**Audience.** Primarily educators and students; also public.

**User problems addressed.**

* Widespread misconceptions about lunar illumination and phases[**\[1\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187118431630049X)**[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/moon_lunar_phases/)[\[5\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa9b0d)[\[31\]](https://www.nsta.org/science-scope/science-scope-january-2019/moon-phases)[\[35\]](https://www.nsta.org/blog/common-moon-misconceptions)**.  
* Teachers’ need for accurate, research‑informed explanations and suggested teaching strategies[**\[3\]**](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198983)**[\[34\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/moonScience/UnknownMoon.pdf)**.

**Description and rationale.**

* For each visualization state (e.g., specific time and site), small contextual explanation panels answer:  
  * “What is happening here?” (e.g., “The Sun is just below the horizon at this crater, leaving it in permanent shadow.”)  
  * “Why is this important for missions?” (e.g., power, thermal, communication implications).  
  * “Common misconception check” (e.g., “You might think the Moon is dark here because Earth is blocking the Sun, but actually…”).  
* Short, teacher‑readable sidebars referencing best‑practice instructional sequences such as the “identify–overturn–replace” strategy for conceptual change[**\[2\]**](https://www.nsta.org/science-teacher/science-teacher-january-2013/moon-misconceptions)**[\[34\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/moonScience/UnknownMoon.pdf)**.

PBS and NSTA emphasize that letting students manipulate models helps them “discover for themselves” but that explicit attention to misconceptions is still necessary[**\[2\]**](https://www.nsta.org/science-teacher/science-teacher-january-2013/moon-misconceptions)**[\[31\]](https://www.nsta.org/science-scope/science-scope-january-2019/moon-phases)[\[35\]](https://www.nsta.org/blog/common-moon-misconceptions)**. Embedding explanations into Stargazer’s interface reduces preparation burden for teachers and supports self‑guided learners.

**Priority.** Core. Without explanation, Stargazer risks becoming “yet another pretty visualization” that does not correct misunderstandings.

### **5.5 High‑Value Enhancement: Scenario‑Based Guided Tours**

**Audience.** Teachers (for lessons), museum/exhibit facilitators, engaged public.

**User problems addressed.**

* Teachers’ limited time to design activities integrating tools like Moon Trek or QuickMap[**\[18\]**](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa9d16)**[\[22\]](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**.  
* Public’s preference for narrative, role‑based experiences[**\[40\]**](https://www.mosi.org/things-to-do/mission-moonbase/)**[\[47\]](https://www.thinglink.com/blog/how-museums-are-using-interactive-media-to-boost-visitor-engagement/)**.

**Description and rationale.**

* Guided “missions” that step the user through a small number of waypoints and interactions, e.g.:  
  * *“Choose an Artemis Base Site”*: compare 2–3 south polar sites to decide which best balances illumination and Earth visibility.  
  * *“Life in a Shackleton Crater Outpost”*: explore how illumination never reaches the crater floor but nearby ridges get near‑continuous light.  
  * *“Revisiting Apollo 11”*: travel from orbit down to the site, see Earth’s apparent motion over a lunar day, and contrast with Artemis sites.  
* Each step includes a prompt or question (for students), a suggested discussion idea (for teachers), and optional “Learn more” for extra context.

Research on interactive museum exhibits shows that technological novelty plus open‑endedness retains attention, but structured prompts enhance learning[**\[47\]**](https://www.thinglink.com/blog/how-museums-are-using-interactive-media-to-boost-visitor-engagement/)**[\[48\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1231234.1231245)[\[71\]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/276016704)**. NASA’s Lunar Nautics and NISE Net games use role‑play and challenges effectively[**\[39\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/lunar_nautics/)**[\[40\]](https://www.mosi.org/things-to-do/mission-moonbase/)[\[81\]](https://www.nisenet.org/moon)**. Stargazer can adapt this to the web context with lightweight, script‑driven tours.

**Priority.** High, but can be iterative. Start with 1–2 tours and expand as time permits.

### **5.6 Enhancement: Educator Mode with Lesson Materials**

**Audience.** Formal and informal educators.

**User problems addressed.**

* Need for standards‑aligned activities and assessments tied to visualization tools[**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[23\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/moon/)[\[27\]](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/resources/nasa-science-for-your-classroom-opportunities-for-educators/)**.  
* Limited time to develop custom lessons and difficulty integrating general‑purpose tools into curricula.

**Description and rationale.**

An “Educator Mode” toggle that reveals:

* Downloadable or copy‑and‑pasteable lesson outlines (learning objectives, estimated time, materials, step sequences).  
* Example student tasks (e.g., “Use Stargazer to compare two sites and justify which to choose for a solar‑powered base.”).  
* Links to aligned official resources (e.g., NASA/LPI guides) where appropriate.

NASA’s education portals (e.g., Infiniscope, LRO Educator Kit) demonstrate a preference for packaging simulations with structured activities[**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[27\]](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/resources/nasa-science-for-your-classroom-opportunities-for-educators/)**. However, building a full curriculum from scratch is likely beyond a hackathon‑scale project; a pragmatic approach is to provide minimal, flexible scaffolds that teachers can adapt.

**Priority.** Secondary but impactful. Initial version could be static PDF or markdown content linked from the interface.

### **5.7 Enhancement: Simple Accessibility and Device‑Friendliness**

**Audience.** All, especially schools and public events with constrained hardware.

**User problems addressed.**

* Processing and graphics demands of existing tools on older hardware[**\[30\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/quickmap/help).  
* Need for inclusive design for users with visual or motor impairments.

**Description and rationale.**

* Design for WebGL performance on mid‑range laptops; graceful degradation (e.g., static images or 2.5D maps) on weaker devices.  
* Interface patterns consistent with accessible visualization guidance (clear labels, text summaries of views, keyboard navigation)[**\[82\]**](https://www.oregon.gov/oha/digital-accessibility/pages/accessible-data-visualizations-quick-guide.aspx)**[\[83\]](https://openfieldx.com/data-visualization-accessibility-tips-for-edtech/)[\[84\]](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/)**.  
* Optional “low‑detail” mode for exhibits or large displays where frame rate takes priority over fine surface textures.

While detailed accessibility guidelines (e.g., W3C ATAG) are generic[**\[85\]**](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/atag/), applying basic principles (high contrast, text alternatives, reduced motion option) can substantially broaden Stargazer’s utility in classroom and public spaces.

**Priority.** Medium. Accessibility should inform technical decisions from the start, but advanced accommodations can be phased in.

---

**66\. Adoption Opportunities**

### **6.1 Schools and Classrooms**

**Realistic opportunities.**

* **Conceptual change units on lunar phases and illumination.** Stargazer can serve as the central visualization in units that follow research‑based sequences for addressing misconceptions[**\[2\]**](https://www.nsta.org/science-teacher/science-teacher-january-2013/moon-misconceptions)**[\[3\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198983)[\[31\]](https://www.nsta.org/science-scope/science-scope-january-2019/moon-phases)[\[34\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/moonScience/UnknownMoon.pdf)[\[35\]](https://www.nsta.org/blog/common-moon-misconceptions)**.  
* **STEM design projects.** Students could use Stargazer to “design” a lunar base site, justifying choices based on terrain, power availability and communications, mirroring NASA’s own student challenges and lunar curricula[**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[23\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/moon/)[\[26\]](https://www.nasa.gov/stem/artemisforstudents)**.  
* **Cross‑curricular projects.** Linking geography (map reading, scale), physics (light/shadows), and language arts (mission narratives) reflects recommendations for cross‑curricular use of lunar missions[**\[25\]**](https://www.k12dive.com/news/3-ways-upcoming-lunar-missions-can-engage-students/703035/)**[\[26\]](https://www.nasa.gov/stem/artemisforstudents)**.

**Key adoption drivers.**

* Browser‑based, no‑install operation compatible with school networks.  
* Short, standards‑aligned lesson outlines that teachers can plug into existing sequences.  
* Clear evidence (or at least plausible reasoning) that the tool directly targets known learning difficulties identified in the literature.

**Unverified opportunities / assumptions.**

* Deep integration into official district or national curricula would require extensive validation and alignment work beyond a hackathon timeframe.  
* Adoption in early primary (below \~grade 4\) is less certain; most research on misconceptions and tool use focuses on upper primary to secondary levels.

### **6.2 Universities**

**Realistic opportunities.**

* **Introductory astronomy and planetary science courses.** Stargazer can provide an accessible alternative to expert tools for introductions to lunar exploration, especially for non‑majors.  
* **Pre‑service teacher training.** Programs documented in the literature already use targeted interventions to improve teacher understanding of lunar phases[**\[3\]**](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198983)**[\[31\]](https://www.nsta.org/science-scope/science-scope-january-2019/moon-phases)**; Stargazer could be used as a contemporary visualization platform within such courses.

**Key adoption drivers.**

* Ease of demonstration in lecture (web‑based, simple controls).  
* Ability to reveal concepts without requiring training in specialized software.

**Unverified opportunities.**

* Research‑grade use for terrain or illumination analysis is not realistic for Stargazer’s scope; professional researchers already have domain‑specific tools.

### **6.3 Science Museums, Planetariums and Public Exhibitions**

**Realistic opportunities.**

* **Touchscreen kiosks** where visitors explore a limited set of sites using the guided tours or 3D explorer, similar to existing exhibits that use Moon Trek[**\[73\]**](https://sites.google.com/francis.edu/earth-to-moon/exhibit-components) or custom interactives[**\[71\]**](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/276016704)**[\[72\]](https://moonshotmuseum.org/exhibits/)**.  
* **Event‑linked installations** during International Observe the Moon Night or Artemis launch events, using Stargazer as a live visual aid[**\[15\]**](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017AGUFMED53H0231B/abstract)**[\[60\]](https://moon.nasa.gov/observe-the-moon-night/resources/moon-trek/)**.  
* **Supplementary material for traveling Moon sculptures** and physical exhibits, providing a digital deep dive into specific features seen on the sculpture.

**Key adoption drivers.**

* Ability to run unattended in a kiosk mode with simplified UI and automatic reset.  
* Narrative‑driven tours that align with an exhibition’s storyline.  
* Visual quality and responsiveness on large displays.

**Unverified opportunities.**

* Direct integration into major museum permanent exhibits would require partnerships and production‑quality robustness beyond a hackathon project; more realistic is use in temporary events, pop‑up exhibits or digital outreach.

### **6.4 Public Science Events and Online Outreach**

**Realistic opportunities.**

* **Interactive component in online talks and livestreams.** Science communicators could share the Stargazer screen while explaining Artemis landing sites, using the time slider and linked perspectives to illustrate points.  
* **Citizen‑science‑adjacent learning.** While Stargazer is not a data collection platform, it can prime users with spatial understanding that would benefit participation in citizen‑science projects related to lunar mapping or mission planning.

**Key adoption drivers.**

* Shareable URLs or configuration “bookmarks” so communicators can link directly to specific scenes.  
* Low barrier to entry: open a link, immediately see something engaging without prior configuration.

---

**77\. Recommendations for the Technical Team**

Below are the five most important, evidence‑anchored findings translated into concrete guidance.

### **7.1 Finding 1: Users Struggle with Lunar Illumination and Phases Due to Spatial Reasoning Gaps**

**Finding.** Students and even teachers widely misunderstand the causes of lunar phases and illumination patterns, with many attributing phases to Earth’s shadow or thinking the Moon makes its own light; these difficulties are linked to challenges in spatial visualization of the Earth‑Moon‑Sun system[**\[1\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187118431630049X)**[\[3\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198983)[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/moon_lunar_phases/)[\[5\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa9b0d)[\[8\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/)[\[37\]](https://doi.org/10.1002/tea.20322)[\[38\]](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/12/5/359)**.

**Evidence.** Multiple studies of pre‑service and in‑service teachers and students report high rates of misconceptions and highlight the role of spatial skills in understanding lunar phases[**\[1\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187118431630049X)**[\[3\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198983)[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/moon_lunar_phases/)[\[5\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa9b0d)[\[8\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/)[\[31\]](https://www.nsta.org/science-scope/science-scope-january-2019/moon-phases)[\[35\]](https://www.nsta.org/blog/common-moon-misconceptions)[\[38\]](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/12/5/359)**. Educational resources from NASA and others stress the difficulty of representing Moon–Earth–Sun movements[**\[6\]**](https://serc.carleton.edu/NAGTWorkshops/visualization/teaching_geospatial/topo_maps.html)**[\[19\]](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/educators/resources/moon/)**.

**User need.** All audiences need tools that concretize abstract spatial relationships and provide correct but accessible conceptual models of illumination and phases.

**Recommendation.** Implement a 3D visualization core with **linked Earth‑and‑space perspectives** and a **time slider** that directly shows how orbital geometry produces phases and illumination at specific landing sites. Ensure every visualization state is accompanied by a short explanatory text explicitly addressing common misconceptions (e.g., why this is not an eclipse).

---

### **7.2 Finding 2: Existing Lunar Tools Are Powerful but Too Complex for Rapid, Non‑Expert Use**

**Finding.** Moon Trek, QuickMap and similar tools are mission‑grade platforms “built for detailed analysis,” and are explicitly noted as often too complex for non‑specialists to use effectively for rapid scenario comparison[**\[12\]**](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/)**[\[13\]](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/details/)[\[55\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/21681376.2019.1577300)[\[56\]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013LPSC...44.2415W/abstract)[\[57\]](https://www.cloudynights.com/topic/597915-lroc-quickmap-lighting/)[\[58\]](http://ltvt.wikispaces.com/)**.

**Evidence.** The Space Apps “Lunar Landing Site Navigator” challenge explicitly names Moon Trek, QuickMap and JPL Horizons as existing tools that are difficult for non‑specialists when comparing landing sites quickly[**\[12\]**](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/)**[\[13\]](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/details/)**. Academic and technical documents corroborate usability and access challenges for expert lunar mapping tools[**\[55\]**](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/21681376.2019.1577300)**[\[56\]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013LPSC...44.2415W/abstract)[\[57\]](https://www.cloudynights.com/topic/597915-lroc-quickmap-lighting/)[\[58\]](http://ltvt.wikispaces.com/)**.

**User need.** Educators, students and the public need a *simplified, opinionated* interface focused on a few high‑value questions rather than a full GIS.

**Recommendation.** Scope Stargazer tightly: limit data layers to those essential for understanding landing‑site selection (terrain, basic illumination, Earth visibility) and provide **guided workflows** (e.g., “Compare two sites” wizard) rather than exposing generic layer pickers or analysis tools. Favor a small set of intuitive controls over completeness.

---

### **7.3 Finding 3: Comparative, Time‑Dependent Landing‑Site Exploration Is an Explicitly Validated Need**

**Finding.** There is a documented need for an intuitive tool that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates quickly, visualizing Sun and Earth positions relative to the horizon over time[**\[13\]**](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/details/)\[14\][**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[50\]](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/featured_sites)[\[64\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20205010352)[\[65\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20190031813)**.

**Evidence.** The Space Apps 2026 Lunar Landing Site Navigator brief directly calls for such a tool[**\[13\]**](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/lunar-landing-site-navigator/details/)\[14\]. LROC’s “Featured Sites” and related resources already implement swipe comparisons and lighting‑condition flip books for Apollo and other sites[**\[50\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/featured_sites). Engineering tools and educator kits provide Earth/Sun visibility and illumination maps for site selection exercises[**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[53\]](https://www.nasa.gov/specials/artemis-south-pole-atlas/)[\[64\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20205010352)[\[65\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20190031813)**.

**User need.** Users want to understand not only *what* a site looks like but *why* it is good or bad at specific times, in direct comparison with alternatives.

**Recommendation.** Make a **landing‑site comparison panel** a central feature: allow side‑by‑side views of 2–3 sites with simple, visual summaries of terrain, illumination window and Earth visibility over user‑selected time ranges. Ensure the time slider is shared across compared sites so patterns are visually obvious.

---

### **7.4 Finding 4: Interactive 3D Visualizations Improve Learning Outcomes and Engagement**

**Finding.** 3D, multi‑perspective visualizations yield higher learning gains and greater enthusiasm in astronomy education than traditional 2D simulations, especially for spatially complex topics like lunar phases; immersive and interactive experiences similarly enhance engagement in informal settings[**\[38\]**](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/12/5/359)**[\[42\]](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/international-journal-of-astronomy-education/article/worldwide-telescope-in-education/)[\[47\]](https://www.thinglink.com/blog/how-museums-are-using-interactive-media-to-boost-visitor-engagement/)[\[48\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1231234.1231245)[\[68\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1286/1/012022)[\[71\]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/276016704)[\[72\]](https://moonshotmuseum.org/exhibits/)**.

**Evidence.** Studies comparing WorldWide Telescope (3D) to 2D simulators report higher learning gains and enthusiasm for the 3D tool[**\[38\]**](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/12/5/359)**[\[42\]](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/international-journal-of-astronomy-education/article/worldwide-telescope-in-education/)**. PBS and AGU reports highlight the benefits of linked perspectives and interactive, student‑controlled models[**\[28\]**](https://www.pbslearningmedia.org/resource/buac19-35-sci-ess-earthsunmoon35model/moon-phases-simulation-viewed-from-earth-and-space/)**[\[29\]](https://www.pbs.org/education/blogs/pbs-in-the-classroom/launch-your-class-to-the-moon-and-back/)**\[93\]. Museum and exhibit research emphasizes the role of interactive media and technological novelty in sustaining engagement[**\[47\]**](https://www.thinglink.com/blog/how-museums-are-using-interactive-media-to-boost-visitor-engagement/)**[\[48\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1231234.1231245)[\[71\]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/276016704)[\[72\]](https://moonshotmuseum.org/exhibits/)**.

**User need.** Learners need to manipulate representations themselves and see immediate, intuitive results to build robust mental models.

**Recommendation.** Prioritize responsive, intuitive 3D interactions:

* Click‑and‑drag rotation, scroll/pinch zoom, and smooth time scrubbing.  
* Clear visual feedback (e.g., subtle motion of Sun and Earth markers as the user scrubs time).  
* Avoid heavy, jagged or low‑FPS experiences that would undermine the benefits of interactivity.

If performance constraints arise, prefer compromising on surface texture fidelity rather than interactivity.

---

### **7.5 Finding 5: Educators Adopt Tools More Readily When They Come with Structured, Scenario‑Based Activities**

**Finding.** Teachers face time and confidence constraints and are more likely to use interactive tools that are packaged with structured activities, prompts and assessments, rather than standalone visualizations[**\[3\]**](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198983)**[\[22\]](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)[\[23\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/moon/)[\[27\]](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/resources/nasa-science-for-your-classroom-opportunities-for-educators/)[\[39\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/lunar_nautics/)[\[40\]](https://www.mosi.org/things-to-do/mission-moonbase/)[\[81\]](https://www.nisenet.org/moon)**.

**Evidence.** NASA’s LRO Educator Resource Kit, Lunar Nautics guide, and K‑12 Artemis activities embed tools within guided challenges and role‑play scenarios[**\[22\]**](https://www.lroc.asu.edu/education)**[\[23\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/moon/)[\[39\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/lunar_nautics/)**. Infiniscope’s Moon phases experiences are explicitly designed as evaluated digital learning experiences, not raw simulations[**\[27\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/resources/nasa-science-for-your-classroom-opportunities-for-educators/). Informal education resources (NISE Net, museum exhibits) mirror this pattern with game‑like or guided interactives[**\[40\]**](https://www.mosi.org/things-to-do/mission-moonbase/)**[\[71\]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/276016704)[\[81\]](https://www.nisenet.org/moon)**.

**User need.** Educators need low‑prep, ready‑to‑run experiences that clearly map to learning goals and are easy to facilitate.

**Recommendation.** From the outset, design **at least one scenario‑based guided tour** (e.g., “Choose an Artemis landing site”) and provide a short, downloadable teacher guide with objectives, step‑by‑step instructions and discussion questions. Build Stargazer’s architecture so additional tours can be added using a simple configuration file or script, allowing growth beyond the hackathon.
